title: Sumedha refuses
hookLine: a princess refuses marriage to a king, cuts her hair and argues her way to the order (Therigatha, Sumedha)

lines: A PRINCESS, PROMISED TO A KING.
cards: A sword, used for a haircut. Sumedha is a king's daughter in the city of Mantavati, and she has been promised in marriage to another king, Anikaratta. She has heard the nuns teach, and she wants to go forth.
Her parents want the wedding. The poem that tells her story is long, and much of it is talk: argument after argument from a young woman who will not be talked out of what she has chosen.

teach.b: First, the argument at home. Sumedha tells her parents she wants to go forth, and they weep and plead: a royal marriage is waiting for her. She answers them with the teaching.

Life is short, she says, and pleasures don't last. She reaches for pictures the Buddha's discourses use for sense pleasures: a dream that ends on waking, goods that are only borrowed. She isn't sulking.
She's making a case. Second, the hair.

teach.h: HAIR CUT, DOORS SHUT, SHE SITS.
teach.b: When the pleading doesn't stop, she cuts off her own hair with a sword, shuts the palace doors, and sits down. The poem says she entered the first stage of meditative absorption, right there. Third, the king.
Anikaratta arrives, dressed for a wedding, with gold and jewels, and offers her wealth and every pleasure a kingdom has. She doesn't run, and she doesn't give in.
She answers him as patiently as she argued with her parents. Fourth, the result.

teach.h: EVEN THE KING ASKS FOR HER.
teach.b: In the poem, the king ends up asking her father to let her go forth.
She wins not by slipping away in the night, but by making her case to every person standing in the doorway, until there is no one left to persuade.
Her refusal is a no to the wedding, and a yes to something she can explain.

how: In Buddhist traditions, going forth as a nun or monk is a decision families take seriously, and the Therigatha's stories of women who argued for it, like Sumedha's, are read as examples of resolve.

o: a princess says no to a wedding, and why
a princess married off against her will
a nun turns away a king's alms offering

used to cut off her hair

s: Sumedha escapes the palace at night to reach the nuns
she stays, shuts the doors, and makes her case to her parents and the king.
she cuts off her own hair before the king arrives
she cuts it with a sword, shuts the doors, and sits in meditation.

games.q: you're Sumedha. your hair is cut, the doors are shut, and the king you were promised to has arrived with gold and jewels, pleading with you. what do you do?
o: slip out the back and run.
answer him, and argue for your choice, calmly.
games.why: she answers him as patiently as she argued with her parents. in the poem, the king himself ends up asking her father to let her go forth.

practice: Bring to mind a choice you've made that someone questions, or that you keep reopening yourself, and say your reasons to yourself plainly, one by one, the way Sumedha laid hers out.
If the decision still stands, let yourself stand with it, calmly, for these breaths; if it doesn't, that's worth knowing too.

wordCard.voice: Sumedha refuses. A princess promised to a king, who cut her hair, shut the doors, and argued until even the king asked that she be let go. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pabbajja: going forth, leaving home for the monastic life. Sumedha argues her way to it.

carryVoice: Your line: she argued her way in. No escape in the night, just reasons, patiently given. Day seven hundred ninety-five, done.
